title: The Return
text:
Drowsy is the afternoon. Beside the narrow fold

the cattle nap. The skittish cow

moos calmly, while the rock blows

the bittersweet nose of the good shy calf...


Seen between brambles is the heated crag

behind which the amate gives its local note.

A westering sun, undecided, designs

on the mother-of-pearl of the sky its bloodied disk.


Along the long dusty solitary road

the voice of the bell tower spreads at length,

and the murmur of the wood and the bull's rebellowing.


And to the native lap of the wild huts

the insinuating girls return from the fountain

shelling in the air their golden cantilenas.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the countryside's late-afternoon return as sound, cattle, and song.

title: Afternoon in the Village
text:
This January afternoon does not have the purity

of that dead afternoon you have already cast into oblivion;

on the same grass, tired, has lain down,

and sick with memories, little sister sadness...


Yet it is the same transparent beauty...

The old bell tower, and the flowering wall,

and the amate raised beside the path

with arms open to humble poverty.


From the houses kneeling beneath the grove,

the afternoon is waving its silk handkerchiefs,

and life in the village treads carpets of calm.


...And I want nothing: I cease being mine,

because over the road —long as weariness—

pursuing your shadow all my soul goes away...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the village stillness and the soul departing after a shadow.

title: Moon at the Hut
text:
To wander, dreaming verses, on silent roads,

with the golden rain of the sun upon your brow;

and seated on a trunk, to gaze at myself for a long time

in the sleeping waters of your glassy eyes...


"And how pretty," peasants would say on seeing you,

those who with their cows go looking for a spring,

and I: "Her eyes look, look more sweetly

than two white stars in evening skies."


And you would smile without any vanity;

then the moon would enter our hut

and, seeing us, the white faithful dog would bark...


Like ripe coffee your mouth would be, mine,

and in the hut with moon, my mouth would drink

in the flower of your lips, an "I love you" of honey.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the rustic romance of hut, moon, dog, coffee, and honey.

title: One Day —God Willing!...
text:
One day —God willing!—

you must love me a little.

I will raise the little hut

where the two of us will live.


What more to ask? With your love,

my hut, a tree, a dog,

and before us the sky and the hill

and the little coffee grove in bloom...


And amid elder aromas,

a mockingbird that would sing

and a pool that would copy

little birds and vines.


What we poor people want,

what we poor people love,

that which we adore so much

because it is what we do not have...


With only that, my life;

with only that:

with my verse, with your kiss,

everything else would be surplus...


Because there is nothing better

than a mountain, a hut, a star,

when one has an "I love you"

and the paths smell of flowers...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the humble wish-list and the repeated enoughness of love.

title: A Hut and a Star
text:

you must love me a little.

where the two of us will live.


What more to ask? With your love,

my hut, a tree, a dog,

and before us the sky and the hill

and the little coffee grove in bloom...


And amid elder aromas,

a mockingbird that will sing

and a pool that would copy

little birds and vines.


What we poor people want,

what we poor people love,

that which we adore so much

because it is what we do not have...


With only that, my life;

with only that:

with my verse, with your kiss,

everything else would be surplus...


Because there is nothing better

than a mountain, a hut, a star,

when one has an "I love you"

and the paths smell of flowers...
editorial_note: This related version preserves the title and the slight tense shift around the singing mockingbird.

title: The Waterfall
text:
Regional scene; burning summer sun;


a graceful parasite hangs its stairway


of butterfly wings, scarlet birds,


on the flowered tower of the shady conacaste.


Such is the stage through which the river runs;


the river that mirrors groves, sky and fronds


and that gleams, at times, like a silver ribbon


that had been embroidered with pearls of dew...


And the river goes singing with a song that enchants:


but on reaching the edge of the abyss, it does not sing,


but imitates the dull clamor of the storm.


And in its crystal, then, golden diadems tremble,


and as it plunges —crying out— its sonorous vertigo,


a hurricane of foams bursts at its feet
editorial_note: The translation keeps the river's shift from song to storm at the brink.

title: Over There...
text:
Lucita, what sorrow

it gives me to see, wrapped in timid flashes

of moon, your fields,

your dark earth;

the hill that rises

with the capulín trees for which you sighed,

and those roads along which you passed

bathed and barefoot!

What sad sorrow!

Your field is in shadows, for you were the light;

and in the cemetery, after you left,

they have put another cross...

One day they said you were lost,

and thorns wounded your own old mother;

and when summer stripped the orchards bare

they found your dear mother asleep,

but with her eyes

open...

You did not understand that the city was

fire that consumes with its wicked lights,

and that it burns the wings

of innocence from little Lucitas...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the rural lament for Lucita and the city as destructive fire.

title: Whitmanic Poem
text:
We children, we

schoolboys,

Girls of North America

workers, students

dominated by lust
editorial_note: The translation keeps the short catalogue and blunt final phrase of the provided Spanish text.

title: Objective Theme
text:
It is true that I write about myself

Who else do I know better?

Where do more blood red roses and kitchen garbage come together

What else has my thick heart, hepatitis or hemorrhoids—

Who else lived my seventy years, my old Naomi?

And if by chance I write about American politics,

wisdom, meditation, theory of art

it is because I read a newspaper loved

the teachers skimmed books and visited a museum
editorial_note: The translation keeps the self-interrogating rush and bodily comedy of the provided text.

title: Butterfly Mind
text:
The mind is like a butterfly

that settles on a rose

or flutters in a heap of stinking feces

dives down to an exhausted bus

or rests on the porch, on a chair, a breathing flower

—open and closed rocking Tennessee breeze—

Flies to Texas to a congress

jumps through weeds in oil fields

Some say these rainbow wings have a soul

others say they are empty brain

tiny automatic wings with great eyes

that fix on the page.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the restless jumps of the mind from rose to refuse to page.
